reference: GNU coreutils date, executed by the harness in reference mode with the same Bash fixture, C locale, and UTC baseline. Each parity case compares the reference status, stdout bytes, stderr policy, and resulting fixture tree against the candidate. The type/help contract case uses documented Bash builtin metadata and the loadable help registration as its independent expectation.
coverage: Default output plus signed epoch seconds and explicit UTC/offset ISO timestamps
Fractional epoch timestamps, including negative and sub-nanosecond values, with GNU %N widths
Local parsing and formatting under a deterministic POSIX timezone rule
GNU ISO-8601, RFC 3339, RFC email, and extended strftime formats
Documented compact, slash-separated, and RFC-style date input shapes
Invalid calendar input statuses and invalid ISO timespec status
Bash type/help metadata for the registered date builtin
exclusions: Current-time output and the documented now input alias are omitted because they depend on wall-clock timing.
Natural-language date arithmetic and GNU options outside the documented loadable interface are not covered.
Setting the system wall clock is deferred; it would mutate clock state and requires a disposable VM or a reviewed clock syscall mock.

cases.purpose: Compare the default output format, signed epoch seconds, Z timestamps, and an explicit +05:30 offset after UTC conversion.
Compare GNU fractional epoch normalization before and after the epoch, including values with more than nine fractional digits, using full and truncated nanosecond formats.
Check local-time interpretation, daylight/standard offset selection, and conversion of an explicit UTC timestamp using a fixed POSIX timezone rule.
Compare epoch, nanosecond precision, colonized UTC offsets, 12/24-hour padding, lowercase meridian, and case-folded weekday formats.
Compare date-only, hours, minutes, and seconds ISO-8601 output plus RFC 3339 and RFC email output for a fixed offset timestamp.
cases.script:
stamp='2024-02-29T12:34:56+05:30'
date -d "$stamp" -I
date -d "$stamp" -Ihours
date -d "$stamp" --iso-8601=minutes
date -d "$stamp" --iso-8601=seconds
date -d "$stamp" --rfc-3339=date
date -d "$stamp" --rfc-3339=seconds
date -d "$stamp" -R

cases.purpose: Compare compact YYYYMMDD, slash-separated date-time, and RFC-style email timestamp parsing against GNU date.
Verify GNU-compatible failure status for invalid Gregorian dates while capturing each diagnostic inside command substitution so wording differences do not obscure the status comparison.
cases.script:
for value in '2024-02-30' '2023-02-29' '2024-04-31T12:00:00Z' '30 Feb 2024 00:00:00 UTC'; do
  rc=0
  diagnostic=$(date -u -d "$value" +%F 2>&1) || rc=$?
  printf '%s:%s\n' "$value" "$rc"
done

cases.purpose: Check GNU date's exit status for an invalid ISO-8601 timespec. Preserve a candidate status difference as a failure.
Confirm Bash reports date as a builtin and exposes its registered help text; this is metadata coverage, not operation coverage.
cases.script:
kind=$(type -t date)
[[ $kind == builtin ]]
help date >/dev/null
printf '%s\n' "$kind" 'help available'

cases.purpose: GNU date can request a system wall-clock change, but exercising that operation here would mutate clock state and the loadable documentation does not advertise it.
cases.reason: Do not execute date -s or another clock-setting path in this environment. A future test requires a disposable VM with an isolated controllable wall clock, or a reviewed clock syscall mock that records the requested timestamp without changing the host clock.
